nameStory: The towhee gets its name from its most common call - a sharp, two-part "tow-HEE" that rises in pitch. This bird is also known as the "chewink" for another of its distinctive calls, and old-timers sometimes called it the "joree bird" for yet another vocalization it makes.
description: The Eastern Towhee is a large, robust sparrow about the size of a robin, with striking black and white plumage on males and rich brown and white on females. Both sexes sport warm rufous (reddish-brown) sides that give them their former name "rufous-sided towhee." These ground-loving birds have a thick, seed-cracking bill and bright red eyes that really stand out. You'll often see them scratching through leaf litter with both feet, making quite a racket as they hunt for food.

idTips.label: Distinctive call
idTips.description: Listen for the clear "drink-your-TEA" song or the sharp "tow-HEE" call that gives the bird its name - once you hear it, you'll never forget it

idTips.label: Ground scratching behavior
idTips.description: Watch for their unique double-footed hop-and-scratch technique through dry leaves - sounds like a small animal rustling around

idTips.label: Male coloring
idTips.description: Males have jet-black head and back contrasting sharply with bright white belly and rusty-orange sides that feel warm to look at

idTips.label: Female coloring
idTips.description: Females wear rich chocolate-brown where males are black, but share the same white belly and rusty sides pattern

idTips.label: Red eyes
idTips.description: Both sexes have striking bright red eyes that seem to glow against their dark head feathers

idTips.label: Size and shape
idTips.description: Larger than most sparrows with a chunky body, thick bill, and longish tail that they often cock upward

habitat: Eastern Towhees love brushy, scrubby areas where forest meets field - think woodland edges, overgrown clearings, and shrubland. You'll find them in dense thickets, young forest growth, and brushy areas under mature trees where they can scratch through leaf litter. They're particularly fond of areas with berry-producing shrubs and dense understory vegetation.

seasonality.spring: Males arrive singing their distinctive "drink-your-TEA" song from prominent perches, while pairs begin nesting low in bushes or on the ground. Listen for increased calling and watch for territorial behavior.
seasonality.summer: Peak nesting season with adults often seen carrying food to hidden nests. Young birds appear later in summer, looking similar to females but with streaky breasts.
seasonality.fall: Northern birds begin migrating south, and you might see increased numbers as migrants pass through. Their scratching behavior is most noticeable as they build up fat reserves for migration.
seasonality.winter: Many birds have migrated south, but some remain in southern New England. Winter birds are quieter but still actively scratch through leaf litter on milder days.

funFact: Eastern Towhees scratch through leaves with such vigor that they can move leaf litter up to 3 inches deep, and their double-footed backward kick is so distinctive that experienced birders can identify them by sound alone - even from inside a house!
confusionNotes: Female towhees might be confused with large brown sparrows, but their size, rusty sides, and ground-scratching behavior set them apart. Remember: "Towhees scratch with both feet, sparrows pick daintily" - plus that unmistakable call gives them away every time.
contextualKnowledge: Eastern Towhees were once considered the same species as the western Spotted Towhee and called "Rufous-sided Towhees." Bird taxonomy can be confusing, and this split happened relatively recently in bird classification history, so older field guides might still show them as one species.
compareHints: Eastern Towhees are the only Pipilo towhee species in New England - their closest relatives are the Spotted Towhee of the west (which has white spots on the back instead of solid coloring) and the Green-tailed Towhee (which is greenish with a rusty cap). Within the sparrow family, Eastern Towhees are much larger and chunkier than most other New England sparrows, with more contrasting colors and that distinctive ground-scratching behavior.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Spotted Towhees differ from their close relative the Eastern Towhee primarily by those diagnostic white spots on wings and back - Eastern Towhees lack these spots entirely.
Unlike its cousin the Eastern Towhee which is boldly patterned in black, white, and rufous with no green coloring, the Green-tailed Towhee is much smaller and more subtly colored overall.
